title: The Confluence of Stone and Syllable

features.name: water-alphabet
features.desc-on-touch: Where two tributaries meet, they write. The rush of water over stone composes itself into syllables. You're reading a river that has learned to be a sentence.

features.name: stone-archive
features.desc-on-touch: The river has carved its own library into bedrock. Every confluence is a word. The stone remembers in grooves—each tributary's dialect preserved as a geological record.

features.name: tributary-voices
features.desc-on-touch: The smaller streams have not forgotten they were once separate. They sing at different pitches as they meet. The confluence is not a merger—it is a conversation between waters that remember their own names.

features.name: written-riverbank
features.desc-on-touch: The banks themselves have become text. Everything the river has ever said is preserved as sediment. You walk on compressed speech, on chapters of water that have turned to stone.

inscription: the river knew how to write before it knew how to flow; the stone listened and learned to remember in the dialect of all the tributaries that still insist they are separate

file.name: River_Confluence_Acoustic_Log_Syllables_Preserved.wav
file.note: Recordings of water over stone at three tributaries where they meet; the frequencies align to form patterns that resemble speech
